title: CompositionLocal, Theming & Design Systems
scopeHtml: Scope: CompositionLocal mechanics and cost, Material 3 theming (color, type, shape, dynamic color, dark mode), LocalContext pitfalls, and building custom design systems on or beside Material.

questions.promptHtml: What is a CompositionLocal, why does Compose have it, and when would you create your own?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you understand implicit data flow in the composition tree and can judge when it is a smell.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A CompositionLocal is a tree-scoped, implicitly passed value. Instead of threading colors, context or density through every parameter list, an ancestor provides a value with CompositionLocalProvider and any descendant reads .current, getting the nearest ancestor's value. MaterialTheme, LocalContext and LocalDensity are all built on it. I create my own only for cross-cutting, tree-scoped data with a sensible default, like design-system tokens. For ordinary data I pass parameters."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Compose's default data flow is explicit: parameters down, events up. That is great for testability but painful for data that nearly every node needs (theme, density, layout direction).

A CompositionLocal is a key. CompositionLocalProvider(LocalFoo provides x) { content() } writes x into a persistent map held by the composition at that group. Children see the map of their nearest provider. Reading LocalFoo.current looks up the key in the current scope's map and, if nothing was provided, returns the default factory's value (or throws if you wrote error(...) in the factory).

setContent
 └ CompositionLocalProvider(LocalContext provides ...)      <- framework
    └ MyTheme  (provides LocalExtendedColors, MaterialTheme locals)
       └ Screen
          └ CompositionLocalProvider(LocalContentColor provides Red)
             └ Text  -> LocalContentColor.current == Red (nearest wins)

Official guidance (developer.android.com, CompositionLocal page) lists the criteria for a good local: it should have a good default (otherwise previews and tests must always provide it), and the concept must be tree- or subhierarchy-scoped, usable by any descendant rather than a few. The docs explicitly call out holding a screen's ViewModel in a CompositionLocal as a bad practice: it hides dependencies and couples every descendant to the VM.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class Spacing(val small: Dp = 4.dp, val medium: Dp = 8.dp, val large: Dp = 16.dp)

val LocalSpacing = compositionLocalOf { Spacing() } // good default => previews just work

@Composable
fun Card2(content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    val s = LocalSpacing.current
    Box(Modifier.padding(s.medium)) { content() }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting a ViewModel, navigator or repository in a local so "everything can reach it". Hidden dependency, untestable in isolation.
  • No default and no fail-fast message: previews crash with an unhelpful "CompositionLocal not present".
  • Using a local for data only two siblings need. Pass a parameter.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does .current return if nothing provided it? → The default factory value; if the factory throws, the composable crashes.
  2. Can a local be provided at multiple levels? → Yes, nearest ancestor wins; this is how LocalContentColor changes per Surface.
  3. Is .current a snapshot-state read? → For compositionLocalOf the read is tracked by the composition (invalidates the reading scope on change); for static ones it is not. See Q122.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "It is like a global you can override in the tree." Senior: frames it as implicit parameters with a cost (hidden dependency, harder debugging), states the two acceptance criteria (default value, tree-scoped), and names alternatives (explicit params, inversion of control via lambdas/slots).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team put a NavController and a ViewModel in locals for convenience. Screenshot tests and previews needed a pile of providers, and moving a composable between graphs broke at runtime, not compile time.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between compositionLocalOf and staticCompositionLocalOf, and how do you choose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Classic Compose-runtime question; separates people who memorized "static is faster" from those who understand invalidation cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "With compositionLocalOf, Compose tracks which composables read .current, so when the provided value changes only those readers recompose. With staticCompositionLocalOf, reads are not tracked, so a changed value recomposes the entire content lambda under the provider. Static is cheaper to read and good for values that essentially never change, like a context or app-level config. For values that change at runtime, like a user-selected theme or a window-size-dependent value, I use compositionLocalOf."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• compositionLocalOf(policy) { default } creates a DynamicProvidableCompositionLocal. Each provider records the value in a state-like holder. A read inside a composable registers that composable's recompose scope as a dependent. When the provider is recomposed with a new value (compared with the policy, structural equality by default), only dependent scopes are invalidated.
  • staticCompositionLocalOf { default } creates a StaticProvidableCompositionLocal. There is no per-read tracking structure. When the provided value changes, the provider's whole content is invalidated and everything beneath it recomposes (child groups that read nothing and have unchanged params may still skip).
  • Trade-off is read cost versus write cost: dynamic pays a small bookkeeping cost on every read (and per reading scope), static pays a large cost on a write but nothing per read. Rule of thumb: many readers + rare writes => static; any frequent change => dynamic. The official page says to use static when the value is highly unlikely to change.
change value at provider
  compositionLocalOf       -> invalidate only readers: [Text][Icon]
  staticCompositionLocalOf -> invalidate whole provider content: [Screen[...everything...]]

Material 3's own LocalColorScheme, LocalTypography, LocalShapes historically use static locals (the issue tracker notes static locals are not recommended for values that change, and Material theming uses them). Whether this is still true in the version you ship: verify in the Material3 source.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Rarely changes, many readers: static
val LocalAppConfig = staticCompositionLocalOf<AppConfig> { error("AppConfig not provided") }

// Changes with user action / window size: dynamic
val LocalWindowInfo2 = compositionLocalOf { WindowInfo2.Default }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Choosing static for "performance" and then re-providing a new value on every theme toggle, recomposing the whole app (Q133).
  • Assuming static means "never recomposes". It means writes are expensive.
  • Allocating a new, non-equal instance on every provider recomposition (Q134).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why would a theme object use static if the user can switch dark mode? → Switching is rare and recomposing the whole tree on a rare toggle is acceptable; reads happen in thousands of places so avoiding per-read tracking wins.
  2. Can you change the equality policy? → compositionLocalOf(neverEqualPolicy()) or referentialEqualityPolicy() are accepted; default is structural.
  3. What happens to remembered state under the provider when static value changes? → Retained; the slot table positions are the same, only the lambda re-executes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE repeats "static for values that don't change". Senior states the mechanism (read tracking vs invalidating the provider's content), the read-versus-write cost trade-off, and measures with Layout Inspector recomposition counts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An app exposed a LocalNetworkState as static; every connectivity flap recomposed the whole screen and dropped frames during a scroll.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through what actually happens when I call CompositionLocalProvider and read .current three levels down. Where is the value stored and how is lookup done?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests depth of runtime understanding beyond API usage; candidates who know about the composer and slot table stand out.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The provider is a composable that starts a group in the slot table and merges its provided values into a persistent map of locals, the 'provider map', stored on the composer for that group. Children compose with that map as their current scope. .current asks the composer for the value of that key from the current map, falling back to the default. For dynamic locals the read also subscribes the current recompose scope. Because the map is persistent, nested providers share structure cheaply."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• CompositionLocalProvider(vararg values) calls startProviders, which computes a new PersistentMap<CompositionLocal<Any?>, ValueHolder<Any?>> from the parent's map plus the new ProvidedValues. The map is stored in the slot table as part of the provider group (so it survives recomposition and is compared with the previous map).
  • current on a local goes through Composer.consume(local), which does currentCompositionLocalScope()[local] and unwraps the holder. Dynamic locals hold the value in a State-like holder (DynamicValueHolder), static locals hold the raw value (StaticValueHolder).
  • On recomposition the composer compares old and new provider maps. If an entry changed: dynamic holders update their state so dependent scopes are invalidated; static ones force the group's content to be treated as changed (the "invalidate all" behaviour).
  • Providing creates a new persistent map each time at that group, so provider expressions should be cheap; they run on every recomposition of the provider.

Version caveat: class names above (ValueHolder, ProvidedValue) are from AOSP runtime source and have been reshuffled across releases; treat names as illustrative and verify in compose/runtime source for your version.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Providers(content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    // Both entries merge into ONE new persistent map for this subtree.
    CompositionLocalProvider(
        LocalSpacing provides Spacing(),
        LocalContentColor provides Color.Red,
        content = content
    )
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing expensive work in the provides argument. It re-executes every time the provider recomposes.
  • Expecting a value provided inside a Dialog/Popup subtree to be visible from outside, or the reverse. Dialogs create their own composition but inherit locals via rememberCompositionContext; custom windows (e.g. a self-made ComposeView on a WindowManager overlay) do not inherit them.
  • Assuming locals cross ComposeView boundaries. A separate ComposeView is a separate composition unless you pass a parent composition context.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a local survive configuration change? → No, composition is rebuilt; values come from the provider re-executing.
  2. What is CompositionLocalContext? → A captured snapshot of the locals, used to re-provide them in another composition (e.g. a custom window), via CompositionLocalProvider(context) { }.
  3. How does LocalContentColor stay correct inside Surface? → Surface provides LocalContentColor using contentColorFor(background); descendants like Text read it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "It is a map you can override." Senior: persistent map in the slot-table provider group, dynamic vs static holders, why provider expressions run per recomposition, and how locals cross dialogs and separate compositions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom floating overlay ComposeView rendered with default colors and wrong density because locals did not propagate; fix was capturing CompositionLocalContext.

questions.promptHtml: What does MaterialTheme actually provide in Material 3, and how does Text end up with the right color and style without being told?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic fluency in the M3 theming model: three systems plus content color plumbing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "MaterialTheme provides three systems through CompositionLocals: colorScheme, typography and shapes, plus text selection colors and the ripple/indication. Components read those. Surface provides LocalContentColor derived from its container color, and Text defaults its color to LocalContentColor and its style to LocalTextStyle, so text on a primary-colored surface automatically uses onPrimary."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• colorScheme: key color roles (primary, secondary, tertiary, error, surface, background, plus Container and on variants). Each key color maps to a tonal palette (13 tones in the official guide) from which the scheme is derived; Material Theme Builder generates Color.kt/Theme.kt.
  • typography: 15 default styles (display/headline/title/body/label x large/medium/small), e.g. bodyLarge Roboto 16/24, titleLarge 22/28 (per the official table).
  • shapes: extraSmall to extraLarge corner scale.
  • Content-color plumbing: Surface(color=...) calls contentColorFor(color) and provides LocalContentColor. Text(color = Color.Unspecified) resolves to LocalContentColor. That is why a Text inside a Button is readable without any color arg.
  • Elevation in M3 is mostly a tonal overlay (tonalElevation) plus shadow (shadowElevation).
MaterialTheme(colorScheme, typography, shapes)
   └ Surface(color=primary)   provides LocalContentColor = onPrimary
        └ Text("x")           color <- LocalContentColor, style <- LocalTextStyle

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun AppTheme(darkTheme: Boolean = isSystemInDarkTheme(), content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    MaterialTheme(
        colorScheme = if (darkTheme) DarkColorScheme else LightColorScheme,
        typography = AppTypography,
        shapes = AppShapes,
        content = content
    )
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Hard-coding Color(0xFF...) in components; breaks dark mode and dynamic color.
  • Pairing wrong roles (tertiaryContainer with primaryContainer text); the official guide shows this as a contrast failure. Always use matching on* roles.
  • Wrapping a screen in Box with Modifier.background(...) instead of Surface, so LocalContentColor stays the default and text becomes unreadable in dark mode.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. M3 Typography has no defaultFontFamily; how do you set a brand font? → Set fontFamily on each TextStyle (per official note), commonly via .copy over defaults.
  2. Why does Text color stay black in my Box background in dark mode? → No Surface, so LocalContentColor is not updated.
  3. Difference between background and surface? → Both are roles; M3 component containers mostly use surface/surfaceContainer roles, background is for the screen backdrop.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists colors/typography/shapes. Senior explains the Surface -> LocalContentColor -> Text chain, role pairing for contrast, and tonal elevation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Dark-mode QA found unreadable black-on-dark text on custom Box containers across 20 screens; the fix was replacing Box+background with Surface.

questions.promptHtml: How does dynamic color work in Compose, what are its constraints, and how would you ship it in a brand-driven app?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests API-level awareness, fallback design, and product judgement about brand versus personalization.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Dynamic color derives a tonal palette from the user's wallpaper on Android 12+ (API 31). In Compose I call dynamicLightColorScheme(context) or dynamicDarkColorScheme(context) when SDK_INT >= S, otherwise fall back to my brand schemes. For a brand-driven app I usually make it opt-in or apply it only partially, keeping brand-critical colors fixed, because the wallpaper can make my brand unrecognisable."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Per the official guide: dynamic color is available on Android 12 and above; below that you must fall back to custom light/dark schemes.
  • The functions take a Context. Use LocalContext.current inside the theme, which is fine here because only resources/system palette are read (see Q128 for Context pitfalls).
  • Dynamic color is generated to meet contrast standards via tonal palettes; if you override individual roles, you take responsibility for contrast.
  • Brand strategies: (1) full dynamic, brand only in logo/illustrations; (2) dynamic plus a custom "extended" token set for brand-fixed colors (success/warning/brand accent) via a custom local; (3) user setting "Use system colors", default off; (4) copy() a dynamic scheme and override primary, accepting contrast re-check.
  • Wallpaper change at runtime: the system triggers a configuration/resource update; the app recomposes with new colors since the scheme is computed in composition (verify behaviour with your activity's configChanges).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun AppTheme(
    darkTheme: Boolean = isSystemInDarkTheme(),
    dynamicColor: Boolean = true,
    content: @Composable () -> Unit
) {
    val context = LocalContext.current
    val scheme = when {
        dynamicColor && Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.S ->
            if (darkTheme) dynamicDarkColorScheme(context) else dynamicLightColorScheme(context)
        darkTheme -> DarkColorScheme
        else -> LightColorScheme
    }
    MaterialTheme(colorScheme = scheme, typography = AppTypography, content = content)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the API 31 gate: NoSuchMethodError/crash on API 29-30 in release devices.
  • Assuming Samsung/OEM devices all produce the same palette. OEM skins may differ; test on real devices.
  • Hard-coded brand red used for "error" while dynamic error is a different hue.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you preview it? → @PreviewDynamicColors annotation exists in compose ui-tooling-preview (verify version), or switch wallpapers on an API 31+ emulator.
  2. Does it work in dark theme? → Yes, separate dynamic dark scheme.
  3. How to keep brand identity? → Fixed brand tokens in an extended theme (Q129) and use dynamic only for neutral/surface roles.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE shows the when block. Senior adds the product trade-off, opt-in setting, extended brand tokens, contrast ownership and OEM testing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Marketing rejected a release because purple wallpapers turned the brand CTA purple; shipped a Settings toggle with dynamic off by default.

questions.promptHtml: How does dark mode work in Compose, how do you support an in-app theme override (System / Light / Dark), and what breaks?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real apps need a user override; tests config-change handling, state persistence and Views interop.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "isSystemInDarkTheme() reads the current uiMode configuration, so the default follows the system. For an override I store a theme preference (DataStore), expose it as state, and pass darkTheme = when(pref){ DARK->true; LIGHT->false; SYSTEM->isSystemInDarkTheme() } into my theme. Compose recomposes immediately without recreating the Activity. If the app also has View screens or splash/system bars, I need AppCompatDelegate.setDefaultNightMode or explicit system-bar styling so both worlds agree."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• isSystemInDarkTheme() is a composable reading LocalConfiguration.current.uiMode. A system dark-mode flip is a configuration change; if the Activity does not declare uiMode in configChanges it is recreated (default). With configChanges="uiMode" the Activity survives and Compose recomposes.
  • Compose-only override: just compute darkTheme from your preference. No Activity recreation needed, so scroll position and remember state persist within the composition.
  • Views/XML parts, Theme.Material3.DayNight themes, WebView, dialogs from Fragments and the window background use the night qualifier from the Activity resources, not your Compose boolean. For consistency, call AppCompatDelegate.setDefaultNightMode(...) (which recreates AppCompat activities) or keep a single mechanism.
  • System bar icon colors in edge-to-edge apps are controlled outside Compose (enableEdgeToEdge(SystemBarStyle...) or WindowInsetsControllerCompat), they will not follow your boolean unless you wire them (insets details belong to the edge-to-edge chunk).
  • Images/vectors: use theme-aware colors, drawable-night, or tint with LocalContentColor.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
enum class ThemePref { SYSTEM, LIGHT, DARK }

@Composable
fun AppRoot(pref: ThemePref) {
    val dark = when (pref) {
        ThemePref.SYSTEM -> isSystemInDarkTheme()
        ThemePref.LIGHT -> false
        ThemePref.DARK -> true
    }
    AppTheme(darkTheme = dark) { Navigation() }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading isSystemInDarkTheme() inside components instead of once in the theme; the in-app override is then ignored in places.
  • Forgetting the status/navigation bar icon appearance, giving white icons on a white bar.
  • Persisting the pref asynchronously and showing a one-frame wrong-theme flash on cold start (read synchronously at startup or show splash until loaded).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you avoid a flash of the wrong theme at launch? → Keep splash until the pref is loaded (SplashScreen API setKeepOnScreenCondition), or cache in a synchronous source.
  2. How do images with hardcoded white backgrounds behave? → They glare; provide night variants or remove baked backgrounds.
  3. How do you test? → @PreviewLightDark, screenshot tests with both modes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Use isSystemInDarkTheme." Senior: explains that it's a uiMode read, a Compose-only override vs AppCompatDelegate for Views, system bar wiring, cold-start flash, and screenshot-test coverage.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Users who picked "Dark" in-app while the phone was in Light saw a dark Compose screen with a white WebView and white status-bar icons.

questions.contextHtml:
Crash dashboard for a 2M-DAU app after a release: ClassCastException: android.view.ContextThemeWrapper cannot be cast to MainActivity (0.4% sessions, concentrated on screens opened from a bottom sheet and from a Dialog) and, separately, a preview that fails with CompositionLocal LocalAnalytics not present. Code:

val LocalAnalytics = staticCompositionLocalOf<Analytics> { error("LocalAnalytics not present") }

@Composable
fun ShareButton(onDone: () -> Unit) {
    val activity = LocalContext.current as MainActivity   // BUG 1
    Button(onClick = {
        activity.launchShare()
        LocalAnalytics.current.log("share")               // BUG 2
        onDone()
    }) { Text("Share") }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find every bug, explain why it only crashes on some screens, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Spots only the cast and "wraps it in a try/catch", misses that .current cannot be called in a click handler, and has no answer for why only some screens fail.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is MainActivity the only host (so is the cast ever legitimate)? Do the failing screens use Dialog, ModalBottomSheet, or a ComposeView in a Fragment/AppCompat context? Do we have a multi-Activity or Compose-in-Service setup? Is LocalAnalytics provided at the root only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the cast with a safe unwrap and move the analytics read to composition scope; ship a patch release or flip a remote kill-switch for the affected sheet if one exists.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) LocalContext.current is not guaranteed to be the Activity; it can be a ContextWrapper/ContextThemeWrapper around it, so a direct cast fails; (b) .current is a composable read and invalid inside the onClick lambda (compile error normally, "works" only if it was hoisted; the posted code is illustrative, the actual bug is reading outside composition); (c) provider is missing in previews/tests because the factory throws; (d) a separately created window/composition without the provider.
  4. How I'd verify each: Stack traces grouped by screen in Crashlytics; log LocalContext.current::class in a debug build on the failing screens; run the preview; unit-test with createComposeRule without providers.
  5. Root cause: LocalContext often returns a ContextThemeWrapper (for example when the theme is overridden or inside dialog/popup hosting). The Activity is at the end of the baseContext chain, not the value itself. The LocalAnalytics read in the lambda cannot happen in composition; reading it into a val first is the fix. The throwing default breaks previews.
  6. Fix:
fun Context.findActivity(): Activity? {
    var c = this
    while (c is ContextWrapper) {
        if (c is Activity) return c
        c = c.baseContext
    }
    return null
}

@Composable
fun ShareButton(onShare: () -> Unit, onDone: () -> Unit) {
    val analytics = LocalAnalytics.current           // read in composition
    Button(onClick = { onShare(); analytics.log("share"); onDone() }) { Text("Share") }
}

Long-term: do not take an Activity in the composable at all; hoist onShare to the screen/holder. For previews provide a no-op default (staticCompositionLocalOf<Analytics> { NoOpAnalytics }) or wrap previews in a PreviewProviders helper. 7. Prevention: Lint/detekt rule banning as Activity on LocalContext.current; preview/screenshot tests for every screen; code-review rule: locals read in composition scope. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not catch ClassCastException. I would not make the default silently no-op for something critical like auth (hides a missing provider); analytics is fine to no-op, an error() default suits app-wide setup.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the composable is shown in a ComposeView hosted in a Service overlay? → No Activity at all; the cast-free design (hoisted lambdas) is the only one that works.
  • Why does it work inside a plain screen? → There the context happens to be the Activity itself.
  • Should LocalAnalytics be static? → Yes, set once at root; a swap (consent change) would recompose everything, so make the instance itself stateful.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shared design-system button cast the context to the host Activity for haptics. It worked for a year, then a dialog-hosted usage crashed at 0.3% of sessions and took two releases to find because the stack looked unrelated.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: wraps in try/catch, does not know contexts can be wrappers.
  • Hire: unwraps via baseContext chain, hoists the read to composition.
  • Strong hire: removes the Activity dependency by hoisting events, explains previews/test defaults, adds lint and screenshot coverage.

questions.promptHtml: What are the pitfalls of LocalContext and LocalLifecycleOwner in Compose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These two locals are used everywhere and misused everywhere; the answer reveals understanding of Context types, leaks and lifecycle scope.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "LocalContext.current is usually the Activity or a wrapper around it, so I never cast it directly; I walk baseContext. I also never store it in a long-lived object, because it is an Activity leak. LocalLifecycleOwner is the lifecycle of the host (Activity/Fragment view), not of a navigation destination or a lazy item, so lifecycle-aware collection or observers should be scoped deliberately. Both are static-like in practice: they change on configuration change because the whole composition is recreated."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Context type: the host (ComponentActivity.setContent or ComposeView) provides LocalContext; themes, dialogs and ContextThemeWrapper can wrap it. LocalContext.current as Activity is a latent crash (Q127). Use findActivity().
  • Leak: passing LocalContext.current into a singleton, a ViewModel or a long-lived callback pins the Activity. Prefer applicationContext (context.applicationContext) for non-UI needs, or avoid Context altogether (stringResource, pluralStringResource).
  • Resource reads and recomposition: LocalContext.current.getString(...) does not re-run on a locale change unless LocalConfiguration is read; stringResource does read configuration. The official sample wraps resources reads in remember(resources, ...).
  • LocalLifecycleOwner: it is the lifecycle of the Activity or, inside a Fragment's ComposeView, the Fragment's view lifecycle owner. In Navigation Compose each back stack entry is its own LifecycleOwner provided to its destination content, so inside a destination LocalLifecycleOwner.current is the entry, not the Activity (verify per navigation version). Package location moved: in newer lifecycle releases it is androidx.lifecycle.compose.LocalLifecycleOwner (earlier in androidx.compose.ui.platform); verify against your lifecycle version.
  • Lifecycle-aware observation: use collectAsStateWithLifecycle() / repeatOnLifecycle rather than collecting in LaunchedEffect without lifecycle, otherwise collection continues while the app is in the background.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun ObserveResume(onResume: () -> Unit) {
    val owner = LocalLifecycleOwner.current
    val current by rememberUpdatedState(onResume)
    DisposableEffect(owner) {
        val obs = LifecycleEventObserver { _, e -> if (e == Lifecycle.Event.ON_RESUME) current() }
        owner.lifecycle.addObserver(obs)
        onDispose { owner.lifecycle.removeObserver(obs) }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• LocalContext.current stored in a ViewModel field (leak after rotation).
  • Observers added without onDispose removal.
  • Assuming LocalLifecycleOwner inside a Dialog or Popup is the destination's; it is inherited from the composition parent, verify in your version.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you get an Activity safely? → findActivity() unwrapping ContextWrapper, or hoist the need as a lambda.
  2. Why prefer stringResource over context.getString? → It reads configuration so it recomposes on locale/font change, and avoids Context plumbing.
  3. A pager page needs "is this page visible" lifecycle, can you use LocalLifecycleOwner? → No; it is the host's, not the page's; use pager state (currentPage) instead.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Get Context with LocalContext." Senior: Context is often a wrapper, leak risk, which lifecycle you actually observe, configuration-change recomposition and API-location changes between versions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An analytics helper held LocalContext.current in a singleton; LeakCanary showed the Activity retained for the whole session.

questions.promptHtml: How do you add custom theme tokens (for example success, warning, brand gradient) on top of Material 3, and what are the options?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Almost every product needs more colors than Material provides; tests knowledge of the sanctioned patterns and their trade-offs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Two sanctioned options from the official docs. For simple additions, extension properties on ColorScheme, Typography or Shapes. For multi-theme tokens I define an @Immutable data class, a staticCompositionLocalOf with a default, a theme function that provides it and then wraps MaterialTheme, and an accessor object like ExtendedTheme.colors. I choose the wrapper approach whenever light and dark differ."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Extension property: val ColorScheme.snackbarAction: Color @Composable get() = if (isSystemInDarkTheme()) Red300 else Red700. Zero plumbing, but it hard-wires the light/dark logic into a getter and cannot be overridden per subtree. The docs recommend it only for straightforward additions or values identical across themes.
  • Wrapped theme with local: the doc example provides LocalExtendedColors then calls MaterialTheme(...). Nesting works the same way as MaterialTheme, so you can override in a subtree (for example an inverse-themed banner).
  • Use in Material components: Material components do not know your tokens, so wrap them (ExtendedButton sets ButtonDefaults.buttonColors(containerColor = ExtendedTheme.colors.caution, ...)) instead of repeating colors at every call site.
  • Annotations: mark token holders @Immutable (or @Stable) so composables taking them skip; with strong skipping the instance-equality rule applies, but the annotation documents intent and keeps older compiler setups correct.
  • Pick static for the local if the token set only changes on theme switch; dynamic if it changes often (Q122).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Immutable
data class ExtendedColors(val success: Color, val onSuccess: Color, val warning: Color)

val LocalExtendedColors = staticCompositionLocalOf {
    ExtendedColors(Color.Unspecified, Color.Unspecified, Color.Unspecified)
}

object AppTheme {
    val extended: ExtendedColors
        @Composable get() = LocalExtendedColors.current
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Color.Unspecified default hides a missing provider as an invisible color in previews; consider visible debug defaults (magenta) or error().
  • Creating the tokens object inline in the theme without remember so a new instance flows every recomposition (Q134).
  • Using extension getters with isSystemInDarkTheme() and then also supporting an in-app override; the getter ignores the override.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not subclass ColorScheme? → It is a final class constructed through factory functions; wrap or extend instead.
  2. Can designers add tokens without code churn? → Generate Color.kt/tokens from Figma variables or Material Theme Builder export.
  3. How do tokens work with dynamic color? → Dynamic scheme replaces Material roles only; extended tokens stay yours (or are derived with harmonization, verify library support).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Add an extension property." Senior: chooses between extension and wrapped local by whether tokens vary per theme/subtree, wraps components to apply them, and handles defaults and stability.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "success" green was an extension getter keyed to isSystemInDarkTheme(); the in-app dark override produced dark text on dark success banners.

questions.promptHtml: You are asked to build a company design system library for Compose used by five apps. How do you structure it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Staff-level API design, layering and long-term maintainability.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Three layers. Tokens (primitive palette to semantic roles to component tokens), a theme that provides them through CompositionLocals, and components that consume only semantic tokens. I decide early whether to build on Material (extend or replace subsystems) or go fully custom, because that decides how much of MaterialTheme, LocalContentColor, ripple and text selection I must replace. The public API is slot-based, versioned with binary-compat checks, and every component has previews and screenshot tests."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Tokens: primitive (Blue500), semantic (colors.actionPrimary), component (button.container). Apps depend on semantic tokens only; rebranding changes primitives.
  • Three paths from the official docs: extend MaterialTheme; replace one or more Material systems while keeping others; or implement a fully custom system. In a fully custom system, MaterialTheme is absent, so Material components lose color/type/shape defaults and the Material ripple/LocalIndication, text selection colors; the docs advise wrapping Material components or writing your own (their Jetsnack sample builds its own button).
  • Provide everything Material would: LocalContentColor, LocalTextStyle, LocalIndication, LocalTextSelectionColors; otherwise a bare Text uses defaults that look wrong.
  • Components: slot APIs (content: @Composable () -> Unit), Modifier as first optional param, state hoisted, Defaults objects for colors/elevation (the Material pattern), small public surface.
  • Stability/perf: immutable token classes, avoid allocating per recomposition, avoid deep nesting of dynamic locals.
  • Distribution: separate module, binary compatibility validator, semantic versioning, sample app, docs, screenshot tests (Paparazzi/Roborazzi style: verify tool choice), lint rules forbidding raw Color(...) and direct MaterialTheme use in app code.
  • Interop: an XML theme adapter or shared resource tokens if Views remain (Q135).
primitives  ->  semantic tokens (light/dark/brand)  ->  CompositionLocals
                                                          |
         components (Button, Card, TextField) read semantic tokens only
                                                          |
                  apps: AppTheme(brand = X) { screens }

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun DsTheme(brand: Brand, darkTheme: Boolean, content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    val colors = remember(brand, darkTheme) { dsColors(brand, darkTheme) }
    CompositionLocalProvider(
        LocalDsColors provides colors,
        LocalDsTypography provides DsTypography,
        LocalContentColor provides colors.onSurface,
        LocalIndication provides ripple(),
        content = content
    )
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaking MaterialTheme into app code so the DS cannot ever drop Material.
  • Exposing every Material parameter in wrappers (huge, unstable API).
  • Forgetting accessibility tokens (min touch target 48dp, focus indication, font scale limits).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Build on Material or custom? → Material saves a lot (a11y, behaviours) if the brand is Material-compatible; custom when shapes/behaviour differ fundamentally.
  2. How do you ship breaking changes? → Deprecation cycle with @Deprecated(ReplaceWith), binary compatibility validator.
  3. How do you stop app teams bypassing the DS? → Lint/detekt rules, code owners, a component request process.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Make a Theme.kt and some reusable composables." Senior: token layers, which Material systems must be re-provided, slot-based API governance, versioning, testing and lint enforcement.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A DS that dropped MaterialTheme but kept using Material Switch rendered default purple until the team wrapped it.

questions.contextHtml: Your app (8M MAU) bumps Compose Material3 from 1.2.x to 1.3.x as part of a BOM upgrade. QA reports: the custom ripple color you set app-wide via LocalRippleTheme is gone on every Material component (buttons, list items, chips), now using default theme colors. The build also prints deprecation warnings for rememberRipple() and RippleTheme. Your own Modifier.clickable wrappers in the DS (indication = rememberRipple(color = Brand)) still show the brand color. A designer asks "why do we have two different ripples on one screen?" Release is in 5 days.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what changed, how you fix it safely, and how you avoid a regression like this.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Pin the old version." Or sprinkles rememberRipple everywhere without understanding the behaviour change.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What exactly did we customise (color, alpha, bounded)? Is the custom color brand-mandated or cosmetic? Do we ship our own components using indication? Are we also on material-ripple directly, and on which material3/wear versions?
  2. Immediate mitigation: From the official migration guide, Material libraries offer a temporary fallback LocalUseFallbackRippleImplementation that makes Material components use the old rememberRipple implementation; I provide it outside MaterialTheme as a stopgap while migrating. The guide says it is temporary, so I do not build on it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Behaviour change: from material 1.7+ / material3 1.3+ / wear-material 1.4+ Material components use the new ripple() Indication node, and LocalRippleTheme no longer affects them; (b) our DS clickable still uses the deprecated rememberRipple path, hence two looks; (c) a mixed dependency set (one module still on the old material3). (Red herring: the Compose compiler or BOM-level overscroll changes.)
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare the dependency report (./gradlew :app:dependencies) for material3/material-ripple versions; read the migration guide diff; screenshot test a Button, a ListItem and a DS clickable; grep for LocalRippleTheme and rememberRipple.
  5. Root cause: Ripple was rebuilt on the Indication/IndicationNodeFactory node API for performance. RippleTheme/LocalRippleTheme are deprecated and not compatible with the new implementation, so Material components stopped reading it; theme-derived values now come from Material theme APIs.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term: replace rememberRipple(...) with ripple(...) from the matching library; configure Material components with LocalRippleConfiguration (color/alpha) via CompositionLocalProvider; on material3 1.5.0-beta01+ the docs mention LocalRippleThemeConfiguration for all components (verify stability for your version).
    • Long-term: in the DS, wrap indication in one DsIndication (ripple(color = ...)) provided as LocalIndication from DsTheme, so all clickable modifiers and Material components share one source.
CompositionLocalProvider(
    LocalRippleConfiguration provides RippleConfiguration(color = Brand, rippleAlpha = RippleAlpha(0.1f, 0.1f, 0.1f, 0.1f))
) { Content() }

(RippleConfiguration and LocalRippleConfiguration are in androidx.compose.material3; they have been marked experimental in some versions, so check the opt-in.) 7. Prevention: Screenshot tests covering pressed state (or a semantic test of the provider), treat deprecation warnings as errors in the DS module, read release notes in the dependency-bump PR template. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not pin Material for 5 days of cosmetic gain: it blocks security/bug fixes; I would not leave the fallback flag in permanently.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does the new ripple affect performance? → The guide says the new Indication APIs bring notable performance improvements (node-based, fewer allocations); I'd confirm with a Macrobenchmark on a scrolling list.
  • Custom design system without Material? → Use createRippleModifierNode from material-ripple (per the guide) to build a themed ripple.
  • Hover/focus states? → New APIs expose them through Indication; check per component.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A DS team bumped Material on a Friday; ripple color regressed on 40 screens. The fix was one provider but the real cost was the missing pressed-state screenshot coverage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: pins the library or hacks per-screen colors.
  • Hire: identifies RippleTheme deprecation, migrates to ripple() and LocalRippleConfiguration.
  • Strong hire: centralises indication in the DS, uses the fallback only as a bridge, adds tests and process safeguards.

questions.promptHtml: How do you customize typography and shapes in Material 3, including a custom font and font scaling concerns?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Practical theming plus accessibility awareness (sp, large font scale).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I pass a custom Typography and Shapes to MaterialTheme. M3 Typography has no default font family parameter, so I set fontFamily on each TextStyle, usually by .copy(fontFamily = Brand) over the defaults. Sizes are in sp so they follow the user's font scale; I verify layouts at 1.3x to 2.0x scale and do not pin heights in dp around text."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Default scale (official table): display 57/45/36, headline 32/28/24, title 22 (Medium)/16/14, body 16/14/12, label 14/12/11, each with a line height (for example bodyLarge 16/24).
  • Customise: Typography(bodyLarge = TextStyle(...)). Unspecified styles keep defaults. Prefer building from Typography() defaults via .copy to keep line heights consistent.
  • Fonts: FontFamily(Font(R.font.brand_regular, FontWeight.Normal), ...); downloadable fonts via Google Fonts provider add a first-use fallback (shows system font until loaded: verify behaviour on your version).
  • Line height: a custom font with different metrics can clip; set lineHeight and consider LineHeightStyle/includeFontPadding options (verify names in your Compose version).
  • Shapes: Shapes(extraSmall..extraLarge) as RoundedCornerShape; components read specific slots (Card -> medium, FAB -> large per the docs' examples). Per-component override is allowed.
  • Font scale: layouts must tolerate scaling; use Modifier.heightIn(min=), avoid fixed height, test with @PreviewFontScale (exists in ui-tooling-preview, verify version). On Android 14+ font scaling is nonlinear for large sizes (platform behaviour, verify).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private val Brand = FontFamily(Font(R.font.brand_regular), Font(R.font.brand_bold, FontWeight.Bold))
private val base = Typography()
val AppTypography = base.copy(
    bodyLarge = base.bodyLarge.copy(fontFamily = Brand),
    titleLarge = base.titleLarge.copy(fontFamily = Brand, fontWeight = FontWeight.SemiBold)
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting fontFamily only for some styles, mixing system and brand fonts.
  • Using dp-based text sizes or fixed row heights (clipped text at large font).
  • Custom shapes ignoring RTL (use RoundedCornerShape(topStart=..) not left/right).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to cap the font scale for a specific element? → Not recommended; if unavoidable, convert with LocalDensity fontScale override on that subtree, and accept a11y complaints.
  2. LocalTextStyle vs MaterialTheme.typography? → The first is the ambient default style (merged via ProvideTextStyle), the second the scale you pick from.
  3. How are shapes used for cutouts? → Custom Shape implementing createOutline.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE changes a font. Senior builds from defaults with .copy, handles metrics/clipping, tests font scale, uses start/end shapes and links tokens to design.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Headlines in a brand font were clipped at 1.5x scale in Arabic; fix was lineHeight plus heightIn(min=) for containers.

questions.contextHtml: A B2B app serves 120 tenants (white-label). Each tenant has its own brand colors, logo and corner radius, fetched at login (about 6 KB JSON). Product wants (1) live preview in an admin screen where the admin drags a color picker 60 times a second, and (2) tenants switchable without restarting the app for QA. The current implementation: val LocalBrand = staticCompositionLocalOf { Brand.Default } provided at the root; the picker mutates the brand state. On a Pixel 6a, the admin screen drops to ~14 fps while dragging; Layout Inspector shows nearly every composable recomposing on each drag event. Median screen has ~900 composables.
questions.promptHtml: Why is this slow and how do you design the theme layer to support both requirements?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use remember" or "switch to compositionLocalOf" without explaining why it helps or what else remains (reads still happen high in the tree).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must the preview apply to the whole app or just a preview pane? What fields change continuously (color only vs shapes/typography)? Does any component derive expensive data from brand (bitmaps, gradients)? Is persisted tenant config static after login?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Scope the live preview to a preview pane (own nested provider) instead of changing the root brand, and debounce commits (apply at drag end or ~100ms).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) static local at the root: every drag event invalidates the entire provider content (900 composables); (b) brand state read high up (val brand by state in the root composable) so the provider re-executes; (c) brand data class not stable or recreated per event; (d) color-derived expensive work in composition (gradients/ColorFilters, tonal palette generation).
  4. How I'd verify each: Layout Inspector recomposition counts before/after; Compose compiler reports for the brand class; System Trace around composition during drag; test with compositionLocalOf as a quick A/B.
  5. Root cause: Static locals invalidate the entire subtree on write. A live preview is the worst case: write rate 60/s.
  6. Fix:
    • Tenant switching (rare): keep static for the tenant theme object. Cost of recomposing the app once per switch is fine.
    • Live preview (frequent): provide a dynamic local only in the preview subtree, or better, make color reads lazy: pass () -> Color or a State<Color> and read in draw phase (Modifier.drawBehind { drawRect(color()) }) so a color change triggers redraw, not recomposition.
    • Compute tonal palettes once per committed color in a remember/ViewModel, off the main thread when heavy.
val LocalBrandPreview = compositionLocalOf { Brand.Default }   // frequent writes
// preview pane only:
CompositionLocalProvider(LocalBrandPreview provides draft) { PreviewPane() }
  1. Prevention: perf budget test (Macrobenchmark with a scripted drag), review rule: any local written more than a few times per session must be dynamic; document local choice in the DS README.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not converting every theme local to dynamic: it adds read-tracking to thousands of reads. Not storing 120 themes in memory; load the active one and cache the last.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the admin wants the whole app live-previewed? → Use dynamic locals for color tokens and draw-phase reads for backgrounds, accept text recomposition, throttle updates.
  • Tenant switch causes a flash? → Cross-fade via animateColorAsState per token only if the cost is acceptable, else a brief scrim.
  • Multi-tenant on tablet with two tenants side by side? → Nested providers; this is why locals beat a global object.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A theme editor ran at 12 fps until the team stopped re-providing the root theme and scoped dynamic updates to the preview pane; fps went back to 55+, no other code changed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot explain why the whole screen recomposes.
  • Hire: static vs dynamic with scoping, debouncing.
  • Strong hire: separates rare vs frequent writes, defers reads to draw phase, adds benchmark guardrails.

questions.contextHtml:
Layout Inspector shows the whole app recomposing about 30 times per second during an unrelated shimmer animation on the home screen (a ShimmerHost composable at the root animates a float). The app's Theme looks like this:

class AppColors(val brand: Color, val surfaces: List<Color>)   // not a data class

val LocalAppColors = staticCompositionLocalOf { AppColors(Color.Red, emptyList()) }

@Composable
fun AppTheme(content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    val shimmer = rememberInfiniteTransition().animateFloat(0f, 1f, infiniteRepeatable(tween(1000)))
    val colors = AppColors(Color(0xFF3366FF), listOf(Color.White, Color.LightGray)) // new instance each time
    CompositionLocalProvider(LocalAppColors provides colors) {
        ShimmerHost(shimmer.value) { content() }   // reads shimmer.value here
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Why does everything recompose, and what are all the fixes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the animation only; suggests derivedStateOf; misses that the provided value is a fresh, non-equal instance on each pass.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Compiler version/strong skipping on? Is ShimmerHost inline? Does content get passed through unchanged? Do we use release builds when measuring?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move the shimmer read out of AppTheme into a lower scope or draw phase; remember the colors instance.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) AppTheme itself recomposes 30x/s because shimmer.value is read in its body; (b) each pass creates a new AppColors with no equals, so the provider sees a changed value; with a static local that invalidates the whole content; (c) List field makes AppColors unstable under older compilers; (d) content lambda recreated.
  4. How I'd verify each: Recomposition counts on AppTheme and leaf Texts; compiler reports (class stability); toggle remember on the instance and watch counts; move the read to graphicsLayer/drawBehind.
  5. Root cause: Reading shimmer.value inside AppTheme makes the theme the recomposing scope. Every pass allocates a new AppColors. Because AppColors is a plain class (reference equality) and the local is static, the provider treats it as changed and invalidates the whole content. (Exact equality used by static locals when comparing provided values: verify in runtime source; either way, a no-equals instance makes this worse.)
  6. Fix:
@Immutable
data class AppColors(val brand: Color, val surfaces: ImmutableList<Color>)

private val Colors = AppColors(Color(0xFF3366FF), persistentListOf(Color.White, Color.LightGray))

@Composable
fun AppTheme(content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    CompositionLocalProvider(LocalAppColors provides Colors) {
        content()
    }
}
// shimmer lives lower, read in draw phase:
Box(Modifier.drawWithContent { drawContent(); drawRect(brush(progress())) })
  1. Prevention: rule "no animated or frequently changing state read in a theme/root scope", compose compiler reports in CI, recomposition-count benchmark on the home screen.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just switch to compositionLocalOf as the main fix: it hides the problem and still recomposes readers. I would not add @Stable blindly on a mutable class.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does strong skipping save us? → It skips composables whose unstable params are the same instance, but a freshly allocated instance every pass is a different instance; the root cause remains.
  • What if colors really do vary per pass? → Dynamic local plus a data class with value equality so identical values are skipped.
  • Debug vs release? → Debug recomposition is slower and masks the proportion; verify in release with R8.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A global "isOnline" banner animation lived in the root scope; the whole app recomposed at 60 Hz until it was moved into its own composable.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sees only the animation.
  • Hire: finds new-instance-per-pass and root read of animated state.
  • Strong hire: fixes both, uses draw-phase reads, adds metrics and benchmark gate.

questions.promptHtml: Your app is half XML, half Compose. How do you keep the theme consistent across Views and Compose, and what are the traps?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Migration reality: two theming systems must agree, and a single source of truth is non-trivial.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Compose does not read the XML theme on its own: MaterialTheme in Compose is separate from the Activity's Theme.Material3.* style. Views inside Compose (AndroidView) use the Activity/context theme, and ComposeView content uses whatever MaterialTheme I provide. I pick one source of truth: usually the Compose tokens, mirrored into XML theme attributes or generated from the same design tokens, or a theme-adapter library that reads the XML attributes to build a ColorScheme. I verify the adapter's maintenance status before depending on it."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Compose to Views: AndroidView(factory = { ctx -> ... }) creates the View with the composition's Context; the View inflates with the Activity (or ContextThemeWrapper) theme, not your MaterialTheme. Dynamic color in Views needs DynamicColors.applyToActivitiesIfAvailable (Material Components) while Compose uses dynamicLightColorScheme; they are separate and can disagree if one is not enabled.
  • Views to Compose: a ComposeView in a Fragment/XML layout needs its own AppTheme { } wrapper; the XML theme does not flow in.
  • Single source of truth options: (a) generate both XML colors.xml/theme attrs and Color.kt from the same token file (Style Dictionary, Figma variables export); (b) a theme-adapter that builds Compose ColorScheme from XML attrs (the Material Compose Theme Adapter library, and Accompanist's older adapter, which is deprecated; verify current status before use); (c) hand-maintain both during a short migration.
  • Dark mode: night qualifier resources for XML versus a boolean for Compose (Q126); keep one mechanism (AppCompatDelegate) while XML screens exist.
  • Typography and shape parity: a TextAppearance in XML versus TextStyle; mismatch is the most common visual regression during migration.
  • Ripples/indications: Views use RippleDrawable, Compose uses Indication; behaviours are close on API 31+, differ on older ones.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ProfileFragment : Fragment() {
    override fun onCreateView(i: LayoutInflater, c: ViewGroup?, s: Bundle?) =
        ComposeView(requireContext()).apply {
            setViewCompositionStrategy(ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed)
            setContent { AppTheme { ProfileScreen() } }   // theme must be re-applied here
        }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting AppTheme around a ComposeView, giving default purple Material colors.
  • Two different "dark" decisions: system for XML, in-app for Compose.
  • Inflating Views in a ComposeView with LocalContext of a different theme wrapper (dialog).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you test parity? → Screenshot tests of the same screen in both implementations, side by side.
  2. How is dynamic color enabled for XML? → Material Components' DynamicColors API on Application/Activity (Android 12+).
  3. What about WebView theming? → Separate: inject CSS or use prefers-color-scheme/force dark; not covered by either system.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Wrap ComposeView with the theme." Senior: names the single-source-of-truth strategy, token generation, dark/dynamic-color divergence and parity testing, and checks adapter-library maintenance.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: During a 40-screen migration, XML screens showed brand blue while Compose screens showed Material default purple for two releases because ComposeViews in fragments missed the theme wrapper.

questions.contextHtml: A release shipped with unreadable text in dark mode on the checkout screen (dark gray text on near-black card) and a clipped total amount at font scale 1.5x. 3% of checkout sessions that week were on dark mode with a large font, and support tickets rose 40%. The team has 400 composable previews, but only default light previews; CI runs unit tests only. Previews sometimes break with CompositionLocal ... not present and take 15+ seconds to render because screens preview with real ViewModels.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: what failed in process and tooling, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Be more careful" or "add more previews" with no automated gate and no change to how previews are written.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which tokens were used on that card (hard-coded or semantic)? Was there a design review in dark mode? Which devices/font scales dominate in the field? Do we have a screenshot-testing tool already?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the card (use onSurface on surface containers via Surface, heightIn(min) for the total) and roll out via staged rollout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) hard-coded colors or Box+background bypassing Surface/LocalContentColor; (b) fixed height on the total row; (c) no coverage of dark and large-font variants; (d) previews unusable because they need ViewModels and providers, so people skipped them. (Red herring: dynamic color; it was off on affected devices.)
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with @PreviewLightDark and @PreviewFontScale; run Accessibility Scanner for contrast; grep for raw Color(; Layout Inspector on a device at font scale 1.5.
  5. Root cause: Process: light-only previews and no automated visual regression, plus components that bypass semantic tokens. Tooling: previews coupled to ViewModels so nobody maintained them.
  6. Fix:
    • Multi-preview annotation: @PreviewLightDark (androidx.compose.ui.tooling.preview; verify availability in your ui-tooling version), @PreviewFontScale, @PreviewScreenSizes, @PreviewDynamicColors for variants. Or a custom annotation combining them.
    • Stateless screen content composables with plain UiState params so previews need no ViewModel and render fast.
    • A single PreviewHost { } that provides the DS theme and default locals; give locals sensible defaults (Q121) so previews do not crash.
    • Screenshot tests in CI (Paparazzi or Roborazzi style tools, verify choice and CI cost) on the DS components and top flows, in light/dark and 1.0x/1.5x.
@Preview(name = "Light") @Preview(name = "Dark", uiMode = Configuration.UI_MODE_NIGHT_YES)
@PreviewFontScale
annotation class ThemePreviews

@ThemePreviews
@Composable
private fun TotalRowPreview() = PreviewHost { TotalRow(UiState.sample()) }
  1. Prevention: lint/detekt rule against raw Color(...) outside the DS; accessibility checks in createComposeRule tests (assertContrast style checks need custom code; use Accessibility Test Framework integration, verify); a design-review checklist including dark and 2.0x.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not screenshot-testing all 400 previews on every PR (slow, flaky diffs): gate DS components and critical flows, nightly for the rest. Not making locals no-op defaults for critical dependencies.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Screenshot tests flake on font rendering? → Pin renderer/fonts, tolerate small thresholds, run on one platform.
  • Interactive previews drift from reality? → Previews are a dev aid, not tests; the CI screenshot is the gate.
  • How do you cover RTL? → Add @Preview(locale = "ar")-style variants for key screens (verify parameter names).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After a similar dark-mode regression a team added one @ThemePreviews annotation and a Roborazzi-style job on 30 DS components; the next two contrast bugs were caught in PR.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the developer, proposes manual QA only.
  • Hire: multi-previews, token discipline, screenshot tests for light/dark/large font.
  • Strong hire: also fixes preview ergonomics (stateless content, default locals), scopes CI cost, adds lint and review checklist.
